The Spotty (Notolabrus celidotus) is a common wrasse from New Zealand coastal waters that undergoes a notable ontogenetic habitat shift during its early life. Newly hatched larvae emerge from demersal eggs with a minuscule body mass of 0.00039 grams [Wwb = 0.00039 grams], reflecting the modest energy reserves contained within the egg yolk at the moment of hatching. This extremely small initial size is typical of labrid fishes, whose pelagic larvae rely on rapid development and efficient first-feeding to navigate the planktonic environment following yolk-sac resorption. Field collections of recently settled juveniles indicate that the total length at which individuals attain sexual maturity is 12 centimeters [Lp = 12 centimeters], a size that is generally achieved within the first two years of benthic life. The onset of puberty, marked by the first visible differentiation of the gonads, is associated with a corresponding wet weight at puberty of 16.3 grams [Wwp = 16.3 grams], calculated from length-weight regressions derived from local populations. This combination of length and mass at maturation positions Notolabrus celidotus as an intermediate species among New Zealand reef fishes, balancing early reproductive investment against the benefits of continued body growth.

Females of Notolabrus celidotus ultimately reach a maximum asymptotic total length of 23.9 centimeters [Li = 23.9 centimeters], a size that typically corresponds to the largest individuals recorded in shallow rocky reef habitats throughout the species range. The corresponding ultimate wet weight attained by these fully grown females is 135.4 grams [Wwi = 135.4 grams], a value derived from the species-specific length-weight allometry that characterizes this wrasse. This maximum body mass places the Spotty among the smaller-bodied labrids of the South Pacific, where related species such as Notolabrus tetricus achieve considerably larger sizes. Growth trajectories for females in temperate New Zealand waters show that the approach to this asymptotic length is gradual, with most individuals reaching approximately 90 percent of their ultimate size by the time they are five to six years old. The reproductive strategy of this species appears to be closely tied to body size, with larger females producing disproportionately more gametes per spawning event. Tag-recapture studies suggest that individual growth rates are strongly modulated by local food availability and water temperature, particularly during the early juvenile phase when mass accumulation is most rapid.

The gonadosomatic index (GSI) has been measured at 10% [GSI = 10%] for actively spawning females maintained at a water temperature of 14.3 °C [T = 14.3 °C]. This value indicates that approximately 10 percent of the female body mass at the time of spawning is composed of ovarian tissue, which is consistent with a batch-spawning iteroparous reproductive mode. The GSI data were collected from individuals sampled during the peak spawning season in northeastern New Zealand, where water temperatures typically remain in this range throughout the austral summer. Histological examination of ovarian tissue from these females confirmed the presence of hydrated oocytes and post-ovulatory follicles, indicative of recent spawning activity.

Longevity records for Notolabrus celidotus indicate a maximum lifespan of 7 years [am = 7 years] under natural conditions at a water temperature of 14.3 °C [T = 14.3 °C], based on otolith increment analysis from a long-term monitoring study. This life span represents a moderate duration among temperate wrasses, placing the species between short-lived annual labrids and the more long-lived Notolabrus fucicola. The age-frequency distributions from sampled populations reveal that very few individuals survive beyond six years, with natural mortality rates increasing sharply after the fifth year of benthic life. This senescence pattern is consistent with a species that invests heavily in repeated reproductive bouts once maturity is reached, rather than deferring reproduction for future seasons. The thermal environment plays a critical role in determining the pace of life history in this species, with populations at the northern edge of the range experiencing faster growth but potentially reduced longevity compared to their southern counterparts. Mark-recapture data from the Hauraki Gulf confirm that the oldest individuals are typically the largest females, which continue to contribute to annual recruitment despite their advanced age.

The reproductive schedule of female Notolabrus celidotus is characterized by a protracted spawning season during which individuals engage in multiple spawning events. Females produce a clutch of pelagic eggs approximately every three to four days during peak activity, with each spawning event yielding several thousand small, transparent eggs. The daily reproduction rate, when averaged across the entire season, results in substantial cumulative fecundity that ensures a steady supply of larvae to the planktonic community. Female wet weight at puberty of approximately 16.3 grams [Wwp = approximately 16.3 grams] marks the threshold at which first spawning becomes possible, though field observations suggest that first-time breeders produce fewer eggs per event than older, larger conspecifics. The total length at puberty of 12 centimeters [Lp = 12 centimeters] is consistently observed across multiple study sites, indicating a robust size threshold for reproductive activation. This consistency suggests that the onset of maturity in Notolabrus celidotus is primarily size-dependent rather than age-dependent, a pattern common among reef fishes where body size directly influences competitive ability and territory acquisition.

A separate assessment of otolith microstructures from fish collected across the Hauraki Gulf and the inner Marlborough Sounds confirms that the age of individuals can be reliably determined from annual increment counts. Growth rates during the juvenile phase exhibit a marked temperature sensitivity, with fish reared under controlled conditions at 14.3 °C [T = 14.3 °C] achieving their asymptotic length earlier than those inhabiting cooler southern waters. This thermal dependence of growth underscores the importance of local environmental conditions in shaping the size-at-age relationships that ultimately determine the reproductive timing of this labrid species.
